title: Go Programming with GoLand
subtitle: Learn Go in GoLand, JetBrains' IDE for Go: types, slices, maps and structs, interfaces and errors, goroutines and channels, tests and a small web service.
outcomes: Set up Go projects with modules in GoLand, and write, run, format and debug programs
Model data with Go's types, slices, maps, structs and methods
Design with small interfaces, and handle errors explicitly with wrapping, errors.Is and errors.As
Write concurrent code with goroutines, channels, select, WaitGroups, mutexes and contexts, and check it with the race detector
Organise code in packages and modules, and test it with table-driven tests, examples and benchmarks
Build and test a small JSON web service with net/http
prerequisites: No Go experience needed, though some programming in any language helps (Python Programming with PyCharm or Java Programming with IntelliJ IDEA is plenty). You need Go 1.24 or later (go.dev/dl) and GoLand on Windows, macOS or Linux: GoLand has a free trial, and JetBrains offers free licences in some cases, such as for students. The race detector needs a C compiler on Linux and Windows.
description:
Go is a small, fast language for building dependable software: command-line tools, network services and the infrastructure much of the cloud runs on. In this course you learn Go the way professionals work with it, in GoLand, JetBrains' IDE for Go. Every lesson teaches part of the language and then shows it in GoLand step by step, with the keyboard shortcuts for macOS, Windows and Linux: creating modules, running and debugging, navigating the standard library, refactoring, quick-fixes, the test runner and the HTTP Client.

You start with types, functions and control flow, then model data with slices, maps and structs, and write flexible code with interfaces and careful error handling. The fourth module covers what Go is famous for: goroutines and channels, select, worker pools, contexts for cancellation, and the race detector. The last module organises code into packages, tests it with table-driven tests, examples and benchmarks, and builds a small JSON web service with net/http. Every module ends with a lab you do in GoLand, and the capstone is a URL shortener service, built to pass a provided test suite under the race detector.

modules.title: Go basics in GoLand
modules.summary: Set up Go and GoLand, write and run your first programs, and learn Go's types, constants, control flow and functions, with GoLand formatting, checking and debugging your code as you go.

lessons.title: Go, GoLand and your first program
objectives: Describe what Go is, and how a Go program is built and run
Create a Go project with a module in GoLand
Run, build and format a program
key_points: Go is a compiled, statically typed language with garbage collection, designed at Google for simple, fast-building, concurrent software. go build turns a program into a single native executable, with no runtime to install alongside it.
A module is a project with a go.mod file at its root, created by go mod init. go.mod names the module (the start of its packages' import paths) and states the Go version, in a line such as go 1.24.7.

Every Go file starts with a package clause. A program starts in func main() in package main; import brings in packages such as fmt, and Go refuses to compile a file with an unused import or local variable.

go run . compiles and runs the package in the current folder, and go build . writes an executable instead. GoLand runs the same tools for you from the gutter and shows the output in the Run tool window.
gofmt gives all Go code one standard layout, with tabs for indentation, so formatting is never up for debate. GoLand's Reformat Code lays Go code out the same way.

lessons.title: Variables, types and constants
objectives: Declare variables with var and :=, and explain zero values
Use Go's basic types and convert between them
Define constants, including enumerations with iota
key_points: var name string declares a variable with its type; inside a function, count := 0 declares one and infers its type from the value. Every variable starts at its type's zero value, such as 0, "", false or nil, so nothing is ever uninitialised.

The basic types include int, float64, bool, string, byte (another name for uint8) and rune (another name for int32, one Unicode code point). Go never converts numeric types automatically: write float64(n) to mix an int with a float64.
Strings are immutable sequences of bytes, usually UTF-8. len(s) counts bytes, not characters, so len("olá") is 4; convert to []rune, or range over the string, to work with characters.
const declares values fixed at compile time. In a const block, iota counts up from 0 on each line, the usual way to define enumerations such as Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of a type Weekday int.
fmt.Printf formats values with verbs: %v for the default format, %d for integers, %.2f for two decimal places, %q for a quoted string and %T for a value's type.

steps.do: In a new project called types, write this program in main.go.
steps.code:
package main

import "fmt"

const daysInWeek = 7

type Weekday int

const (
	Monday Weekday = iota
	Tuesday
	Wednesday
)

func main() {
	var count int   // zero value: 0
	var name string // zero value: ""
	price := 2.5    // float64, inferred from the value
	ok := true
	fmt.Println(count, name == "", price, ok)

	total := float64(daysInWeek) * price // conversions are always explicit
	fmt.Printf("%.2f %T\n", total, total)

	word := "olá"
	fmt.Println(len("Lisboa"), len(word)) // len counts bytes
	fmt.Println(len([]rune(word)))        // runes: the characters
	fmt.Printf("%q %v %d\n", word, Wednesday, Wednesday)
}

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: 0 true 2.5 true, then 17.50 float64, 6 4, 3, and "olá" 2 2.

steps.do: Put the caret on price and open its quick documentation to see the type Go inferred.
steps.see: price is a float64.

lessons.title: Control flow and functions
objectives: Write if, for and switch statements in Go's style
Write functions with several results and variadic parameters
Use defer, and step through code in GoLand's debugger
key_points: if needs no parentheses but always has braces, and can start with a short statement whose variables exist only inside the if and its else, as in if n, err := strconv.Atoi(s); err == nil { ... }.

for is Go's only loop: the three-part for i := 0; i < n; i++, the condition-only for x < 10, the endless for { }, and for range over slices, maps, strings, channels and, since Go 1.22, integers (for i := range 3).
switch compares a value with each case, or, with no value, tests each case's condition in turn. Only the first matching case runs: there's no fall-through unless you write fallthrough.
A function can return several values, such as a result and an error, and its results can be named. A variadic parameter, as in sum(numbers ...int), takes any number of arguments as a slice.
defer schedules a call to run when the surrounding function returns, in last-in, first-out order, with its arguments evaluated straight away. It's the usual way to close files and release locks.

modules.title: Slices, maps and structs
modules.summary: Store and organise data the Go way: slices and the arrays behind them, maps and the comma-ok idiom, and structs with methods, pointer receivers and embedding.

lessons.title: Arrays and slices
objectives: Explain how a slice relates to its underlying array
Create, grow and copy slices with make, append and slices.Clone
Sort and search slices with the slices package
key_points: An array has a fixed length that is part of its type, such as [3]int, and is copied when assigned. Most code uses slices instead: a slice is a view of an array, made of a pointer, a length (len) and a capacity (cap).
append(s, x) adds elements and returns the slice, which may now use a new, larger array if the old one was full, so always assign the result back: s = append(s, x).
Slicing, as in s[1:3], makes a slice that shares the same array, so writing through one is visible through the other. When you need an independent copy, use slices.Clone(s) or copy(dst, src).
make([]int, 0, 10) creates an empty slice with room for 10 elements, which saves reallocations when you know the size. A nil slice (var s []int) has length 0 and works with len, append and range.
for i, v := range s gives each index and a copy of each element. The slices package (Go 1.21+) has generic helpers such as slices.Sort, slices.Contains, slices.Index and slices.Max.

steps.do: Create a project called slicesdemo (not slices: a module shouldn't share a standard library package's name) and write this program.
steps.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"slices"
)

func main() {
	scores := []int{72, 95, 64}
	scores = append(scores, 88)
	fmt.Println(scores, len(scores))

	top := scores[1:3] // a view of the same underlying array
	top[0] = 100
	fmt.Println(scores, top)

	safe := slices.Clone(scores[1:3]) // an independent copy
	safe[0] = 0
	fmt.Println(scores, safe)

	squares := make([]int, 0, 10) // length 0, room for 10
	for i := range 5 {
		squares = append(squares, i*i)
	}
	fmt.Println(squares, len(squares), cap(squares))

	slices.Sort(scores)
	fmt.Println(scores, slices.Contains(scores, 64), slices.Index(scores, 88))

	var none []int
	fmt.Println(none == nil, len(none))
}

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: [72 95 64 88] 4, then [72 100 64 88] [100 64]: writing through top changed scores; then [72 100 64 88] [0 64]: the clone is independent.

lessons.title: Maps
objectives: Create maps, and read, write and delete entries
Tell a missing key from a zero value with the comma-ok form
Iterate over a map in a predictable order
key_points: A map[K]V holds key-value pairs, with keys of any comparable type. Create one with a literal, map[string]int{}, or with make(map[string]int), then read and write entries with m[key].
Reading a missing key gives the value type's zero value, which makes counting easy (counts[word]++). To tell a missing key from a stored zero, use the comma-ok form: v, ok := m[key].
delete(m, key) removes an entry and len(m) counts them. A nil map, declared with var m map[string]int, can be read, but writing to it panics with assignment to entry in nil map.

Ranging over a map visits its entries in an unspecified order that can change from run to run. For a stable order, sort the keys first, for example with slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m)) in Go 1.23 or later.
A map passed to a function is shared, not copied, so the function can change the caller's map. Maps aren't safe for concurrent writes: protect one with a mutex when goroutines share it (module 4).

lessons.title: Structs and methods
objectives: Define struct types and create values of them
Write methods with value and pointer receivers
Compose types by embedding
key_points: A struct groups named fields, as in type Player struct { Name string; Score int }. Create one with a literal, Player{Name: "Ana"}; fields you leave out get their zero values.

A method is a function with a receiver: func (p Player) Describe() string. A value receiver works on a copy; a pointer receiver, func (p *Player) Move(dx, dy int), can change the original and avoids copying large structs.
Go has no constructors: by convention, a function such as NewPlayer(name string) *Player builds and returns a ready-to-use value. &Player{...} creates a struct and gives a pointer to it.
Fields are reached the same way through a value or a pointer (p.Score): Go follows the pointer for you, and calls pointer methods on addressable values, such as variables, automatically.
Embedding a type, as in type Captain struct { Player; Team string }, gives Captain all of Player's fields and methods, which are promoted. It's composition, not inheritance: a Captain isn't a Player.
Assigning a struct copies all its fields, so changing the copy leaves the original alone; likewise a range loop's variable is a copy of each element, so change elements through their index.

modules.title: Interfaces and errors
modules.summary: Write flexible code with small interfaces that types satisfy implicitly, and handle failure the Go way: errors as values, wrapped with context and inspected with errors.Is and errors.As.

lessons.title: Interfaces
objectives: Define an interface and satisfy it implicitly
Use type assertions and type switches
Recognise common standard interfaces, such as fmt.Stringer and io.Reader
key_points: An interface lists method signatures, as in type Shape interface { Area() float64 }. Any type with those methods satisfies it automatically: there's no implements keyword, so a type and the interfaces it satisfies can live in different packages.

Go favours small interfaces, often of a single method, such as fmt.Stringer (String() string), io.Reader (Read(p []byte) (n int, err error)) and error itself. Small interfaces are easy to satisfy and easy to fake in tests.

An interface value holds a concrete type and a value. A type assertion, r, ok := s.(Rect), takes the concrete value out, with ok false if it isn't one; a type switch, switch v := s.(type), handles several types.
An interface value is nil only if it holds no type at all: an interface holding a nil pointer is not nil, a classic cause of surprising err != nil results.
any is another name for interface{}, which every type satisfies. Since Go 1.18, generic functions use interfaces as constraints on type parameters, as in func Max[T cmp.Ordered](a, b T) T.
A good rule of thumb is to accept interfaces and return concrete types: a function that takes the smallest interface it needs works with more types and is easier to test.

lessons.title: Errors
objectives: Return and check errors the Go way
Wrap errors with context, and inspect them with errors.Is and errors.As
Know when panic and recover are appropriate
key_points: In Go, errors are values: a function that can fail returns an error as its last result, and the caller checks it at once with if err != nil, handling or returning it. error is an interface with one method, Error() string.

errors.New("not found") makes a simple error, and package-level ones such as io.EOF are sentinel errors that callers compare against. fmt.Errorf with %w wraps an error, adding context and keeping the original inside.

errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) reports whether err is, or wraps, that error; use it rather than ==, which misses wrapped errors. errors.As(err, &target) finds a wrapped error of a given type, such as *RangeError, to read its fields.
A custom error type is any type with an Error() string method. Give it an Unwrap() error method if it wraps another error, so that errors.Is and errors.As can look inside.
Add context as an error travels up, as in fmt.Errorf("load config: %w", err), and handle it once, in one place: log it or report it, rather than logging it at every level.

panic stops normal execution and unwinds the stack, running deferred calls, and recover inside a deferred function can stop it. Keep panics for bugs that should never happen, not for expected failures such as bad input.

modules.title: Goroutines and channels
modules.summary: Run work concurrently with goroutines, coordinate it with WaitGroups, mutexes and channels, choose between channels with select, cancel work with contexts, and catch data races with the race detector.

lessons.title: Goroutines, WaitGroups and mutexes
objectives: Start goroutines and wait for them with sync.WaitGroup
Protect shared data with sync.Mutex
Find data races with the race detector
key_points: go f(x) starts f running concurrently in a new goroutine, and the caller carries on at once. Goroutines are cheap: each starts with a small stack that grows as needed, and the Go runtime schedules them across operating-system threads.

A program ends when main returns, even if other goroutines are still running. sync.WaitGroup waits for a group: wg.Add(1) before starting each goroutine, defer wg.Done() inside it, and wg.Wait() to block until all have finished.
Since Go 1.22, each iteration of a for loop has its own loop variable, so a goroutine started in the loop sees that iteration's value; older code had to copy it first (i := i).
When goroutines share data and at least one of them writes, access must be synchronised. sync.Mutex does it: mu.Lock() before touching the data and mu.Unlock() after, often with defer mu.Unlock().

A data race is unsynchronised access from two goroutines, at least one of them a write, and its result is undefined. The race detector, go run -race or go test -race, reports races that happen while the program runs, with both goroutines' stacks.
Go 1.25 added wg.Go(f), which does the Add, the go statement and the Done for you. With Go 1.24, write the three steps yourself.

lessons.title: Channels
objectives: Send and receive values over unbuffered and buffered channels
Close channels and range over them
Recognise and avoid deadlocks
key_points: A channel passes values between goroutines: make(chan int) creates one, ch <- v sends and v := <-ch receives. Sharing data by communicating like this avoids most locking.

On an unbuffered channel a send waits until another goroutine receives, so the two meet and synchronise. A buffered channel, make(chan string, 2), accepts sends without waiting until its buffer is full.
The sender closes a channel with close(ch) to say no more values are coming. for v := range ch receives until the channel is closed and empty, and v, ok := <-ch gives ok == false once it is.
Sending on a closed channel panics, so only the sender closes a channel, and only once. Receivers don't close channels, and a channel that's never closed is simply garbage-collected.
Direction types document intent, and the compiler enforces them: a chan<- int can only send and a <-chan int can only receive, as in func produce(n int, out chan<- int).
If every goroutine is blocked waiting, the runtime stops the program with fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!: a send or receive that nothing will ever match.

steps.do: In a project called channels, write this program.
Run it.
steps.see: sum 15, then first second, then 0 false: a closed channel gives the zero value and false.

steps.do: In a project called deadlock, write this program and run it.
steps.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	ch := make(chan int)
	ch <- 1 // nobody is receiving: this send waits for ever
	fmt.Println(<-ch)
}
steps.see: fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock! and goroutine 1 [chan send], pointing at the line ch <- 1.

steps.do: Give the channel a buffer, make(chan int, 1), and run it again.
Back in channels, put a breakpoint inside produce and debug. In the Debug tool window, switch between goroutines: main's goroutine and produce's each have their own stack.

lessons.title: select, worker pools and context
objectives: Wait on several channels at once with select
Build a worker pool with jobs and results channels
Cancel work and set deadlines with context
key_points: select waits on several channel operations and runs the first that's ready, choosing at random if several are. A default case makes it non-blocking, and a case on time.After(d) gives up after a while.

A worker pool starts a fixed number of goroutines that take jobs from one channel and send results on another. Close jobs once every job is sent, and close results after wg.Wait() in a goroutine of its own, so the reader's range ends.

context.Context carries cancellation and deadlines across calls and goroutines. context.WithTimeout(parent, d) returns a context that's done after d and a cancel function you must call, usually with defer cancel().
A function that may take long takes a ctx as its first parameter and watches <-ctx.Done() in a select; ctx.Err() then says why it ended: context.Canceled or context.DeadlineExceeded.
Limit concurrency to what the work needs: a worker pool, or a buffered channel used as a semaphore, stops a program starting thousands of goroutines that all hit the same server or disk.

walkthrough.title: A worker pool with a deadline

steps.do: In a project called pool, write this program: three workers take six jobs, where job n takes n × 50 ms, all under a 275 ms deadline.
Run it.
steps.see: job 1: done to job 4: done, then job 5 and job 6: context deadline exceeded.

steps.see: With 500 ms all six jobs finish; with 120 ms only jobs 1 and 2 do.

steps.do: Put the caret on WithTimeout and read its documentation, including why cancel must be called.
Check that the pool is free of races.
steps.code: go run -race .
steps.see: The same output, with no DATA RACE warning.

lab.title: Check websites concurrently
lab.goal: Write a worker pool that checks twelve pretend websites four at a time, with a timeout on each check, then find and fix a data race with the race detector.
setup: GoLand, and a new project called sitecheck with its main.go replaced by the starter file
For the race detector: a C compiler on Linux (gcc) or Windows (such as MinGW-w64 gcc); on macOS it works without one. Without it, read the -race steps rather than running them.

hints: Call wg.Add(1) before the go statement, not inside the goroutine, or Wait might run before Add.
ctx.Err() is context.DeadlineExceeded when a WithTimeout context runs out of time, so errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) spots a timeout.
If the program hangs, results is never closed: the goroutine that calls wg.Wait() must then call close(results).

modules.title: Packages, testing and a web service
modules.summary: Organise code in packages and modules, test it with go test (table-driven tests, examples, coverage and benchmarks), and build and test a small JSON web service with net/http.

lessons.title: Packages and modules
objectives: Organise a module into packages, and control what's exported
Manage dependencies with go get and go mod tidy
Check code with go vet
key_points: A package is a folder of .go files that share a package name, and a module is a tree of packages with a go.mod at its root. A package's import path is the module path plus its folder, such as example.com/greet/internal/words.

Names that start with a capital letter (Greeting) are exported and usable from other packages; lower-case names (shout) are private to their package, and using one from outside fails with name shout not exported by package words.
A package under a folder named internal can only be imported by code in the tree rooted at internal's parent folder, which keeps it private to your module.

go get example.com/pkg@v1.2.3 adds or updates a dependency in go.mod, and go.sum records checksums of the downloaded code; go mod tidy adds what the code imports and removes what it no longer needs. Commit both files.
Don't use a standard library package's name, such as slices or structs, as a module path: the go command reports an ambiguous import. Keep package names short, lower-case and singular.
go vet ./... reports suspicious code that still compiles, such as Printf calls whose arguments don't match their format; ./... means every package in the module.

walkthrough.title: A module with an internal package

steps.do: Create a project called greet, and change the first line of go.mod to a full module path.
steps.code: module example.com/greet

steps.do: Create the folders internal/words in the Project tool window, then a Go file words.go inside them, and write the package.
Write main.go, importing the package by its path. GoLand offers to add the import as you type words.
Run it.
steps.see: Olá, Ana!

steps.see: GoLand marks the error straight away; go build would say name shout not exported by package words. Change it back.

lessons.title: Testing with go test
objectives: Write table-driven tests with subtests
Run tests, read failures and measure coverage in GoLand
Write examples and benchmarks
key_points: Tests live in files ending _test.go, next to the code they test. A test is func TestXxx(t *testing.T); t.Errorf reports a failure and carries on, while t.Fatalf reports one and stops that test.

A table-driven test lists its cases in a slice of structs and loops over them, running each with t.Run(name, ...) as a subtest, so a failure names its case (spaces become underscores, as in TestWordCount/extra_spaces).
go test ./... runs every package's tests: -v lists each test, -run picks tests by a regular expression, -race adds the race detector, and -cover reports the percentage of statements the tests ran.
An example, a func ExampleReverse() ending with an // Output: comment, runs as a test that compares what it prints, and appears in the package's documentation.

A benchmark is func BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B). Go 1.24 added for b.Loop() { ... } as its loop; older code loops for i := 0; i < b.N; i++. Run benchmarks with go test -bench=. and read the ns/op column.

steps.do: Create a project with the module path example.com/textutil and write textutil.go.
With the caret in WordCount, open the Generate menu and choose to generate a test for the function: GoLand creates textutil_test.go with a table-driven skeleton.
Replace the generated file's contents with these tests.
Run the tests from the gutter icon beside TestWordCount, or from the caret in it.
steps.see: A test tree with TestWordCount and its four subtests, all passed.

steps.do: Break a case on purpose: change the want for extra spaces to 3, and rerun.
steps.see: --- FAIL: TestWordCount/extra_spaces with WordCount("  hello   world ") = 2, want 3. Put it back.

steps.do: Jump between the code and its test.
From the gutter icon's menu, choose Run with Coverage, and look at the coloured bars beside textutil.go's lines.
In the Terminal, run everything verbosely, then with coverage, then the benchmark.
steps.code:
go test -v ./...
go test -cover ./...
go test -bench=. -run='^$' ./...
steps.see: ok  example.com/textutil, then coverage: 100.0% of statements, then a BenchmarkWordCount line with ns/op, whose numbers depend on your computer.

lessons.title: A small web service with net/http
objectives: Route requests with http.ServeMux patterns, including methods and path values
Read and write JSON in handlers
Test handlers with httptest, and call the service from GoLand's HTTP Client
key_points: net/http in the standard library is enough for real services. A handler is a func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request), and http.ListenAndServe(addr, handler) serves requests, each in its own goroutine.

Since Go 1.22, http.ServeMux patterns can name a method and wildcards, as in mux.HandleFunc("GET /tasks/{id}", h). r.PathValue("id") reads the wildcard, and a request with the wrong method gets 405 Method Not Allowed.

encoding/json maps structs to JSON using field tags such as `json:"title"`, and only exported fields are encoded. json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&v) reads a request body; json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v) writes a response.

Set headers before writing the body: w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json"), then w.WriteHeader(http.StatusCreated) for any status other than 200. http.Error(w, msg, code) sends a plain-text error.

Handlers run concurrently, so shared state such as an in-memory store needs a sync.Mutex. net/http/httptest tests handlers without a network: httptest.NewRecorder() records the response to httptest.NewRequest(...).
GoLand's HTTP Client runs requests written in .http files, such as GET http://localhost:8080/hello/Ana, straight from the editor, and shows each response.

project.title: Build a URL shortener service
project.brief: Build a small URL shortener in Go: a JSON web service that turns long links into short codes, redirects visitors and counts their visits. The provided shortener_test.go describes the service: write NewHandler() http.Handler so that every test passes, including under the race detector. POST /links with {"url": "https://go.dev/doc/"} replies 201 Created with the new code and the URL; only absolute http and https URLs are accepted, and anything else gets 400 with a JSON error. GET /{code} redirects with 302 Found to the stored URL and counts the visit, and unknown codes get 404. GET /links/{code} replies with the code, the URL and the number of visits. Structure the module like a professional project: keep storage in its own package behind a small interface (so a database could replace the in-memory map later), use a mutex wherever goroutines share data, wrap errors with context, and add table-driven tests of your own, an example and a benchmark. Run the service and try every endpoint from GoLand's HTTP Client.
deliverables: A module with a main package and at least one internal package, such as internal/store, formatted with gofmt and clean under go vet
NewHandler() http.Handler, passing the provided tests with go test -race ./...
Table-driven tests of your own (for URL validation and the store), an Example and a Benchmark, covering at least 80% of statements
A requests.http file that exercises every endpoint, with the responses it produced
A README explaining the design: the packages, the storage interface, how concurrency is made safe and how codes are generated

rubric.name: Correctness
rubric.description: All provided tests pass under the race detector, and responses use the right status codes, headers and JSON.

rubric.name: Design and packages
rubric.description: Clear packages with small exported APIs, a storage interface, and handlers kept separate from storage.

rubric.name: Errors and validation
rubric.description: Bad input is rejected with helpful JSON errors, and errors are wrapped with context and checked with errors.Is or errors.As.

rubric.name: Concurrency safety
rubric.description: Shared state is protected, there are no data races, and visit counts stay exact under concurrent requests.

rubric.name: Tests
rubric.description: Readable, independent table-driven tests, an example and a benchmark, with coverage of at least 80%.

rubric.name: Code quality
rubric.description: gofmt and go vet clean, idiomatic names, documentation comments on exported names, and a useful README.

project.submit: Paste the output of go test -race -cover ./... and go vet ./..., your handler and store code, your requests.http with its responses, and the README.
